In North Carolina (climate zone 3A), as shown in Figures 2(a) and 2(b), the upgrades significantly lower summer cooling peaks in the afternoon as well as winter heating peaks in the morning and evening. In Hawai‘i (climate zone 1A), as shown in Figure 2(c), the upgrades help reduce cooling loads throughout the day. For the example dwelling in Hawai‘i, the sudden spikes in cooling energy consumption at 3:15 and 22:15, and the sharp drops at 7:15 and 12:15, are driven by changes in the cooling setpoint temperature. At 3:00 and 22:00, the setpoint decreases—from 67.5°F to 66°F and from 70°F to 67.5°F, respectively—triggering increased cooling energy use over the following 15 minutes. In contrast, at 7:00 and 12:00, the setpoint rises—from 66°F to 68.5°F and from 68.5°F to 70°F—eliminating the cooling demand and resulting in zero energy use for the next 15 minutes. In Alaska (climate zone 8AK), as shown in Figure 2(d), the upgrades result in a steady reduction in baseline heating energy use across all hours. Overall, the results demonstrate that duct sealing and insulation upgrades are effective in improving energy efficiency across a range of climates, especially during periods of high thermal demand. 9 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. Heating and cooling energy consumption 15-minute time-series data before and after the duct sealing and insulation upgrade 4.2 Stock Energy Impacts 4.2.1 Annual Stock Energy Analysis Figure 3 shows the annual site energy consumption by end use before and after the duct sealing and insulation upgrade for all homes. The annual stock energy savings is 240 TWh, compared to a pre-upgrade consumption of 3,454 TWh—representing a 7% reduction. Most savings occurred in heating and cooling end uses. These include 8% (22 TWh) electricity heating savings, 11% (129 TWh) natural gas heating savings, 8% (14 TWh) fuel oil heating savings, 10% (13 TWh) propane heating savings, 35% (8 TWh) electricity heat pump backup heating savings, 11% (43 TWh) electricity cooling savings, 12% (4 TWh) electricity heating fans and pumps savings, and 13% (9 TWh) electricity cooling fans and pumps savings. 10 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications.
